claim: The quadratic color model (QCM) explains the same cross-validated variance as a conventional general linear model (GLM) with far fewer free parameters when modeling V1 BOLD fMRI responses to chromatic modulations.
source: We find that the QCM explains the same, cross-validated variance as a conventional general linear model, with far fewer free parameters.
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-validation analysis comparing QCM (6 parameters) to GLM (41 parameters) as shown in Figure 4 and described in the Results section.

claim: The QCM generalizes to allow prediction of V1 responses to a large range of chromatic modulations.
source: The QCM generalizes to allow prediction of V1 responses to a large range of modulations.
evidence: Supported by leave-session-out cross-validation results shown in Figure 5 and supplementary figures, demonstrating prediction of responses to untested chromatic directions.

claim: Results replicate well for each subject across both measurement sets.
source: We replicate the results for each subject and find good agreement across both replications and subjects.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison of Measurement Set 1 and 2 results across all three subjects in Figures 2, 6, 7, and throughout the Results section.

claim: Within the LM cone contrast plane, V1 is most sensitive to L-M contrast modulations.
source: We find that within the LM cone contrast plane, V1 is most sensitive to L-M contrast modulations and least sensitive to L+M contrast modulations.
evidence: Supported by elliptical isoresponse contours with minor axis aligned to L-M direction (Figure 6) and contrast response functions (Figure 2).

claim: Within the LM cone contrast plane, V1 is least sensitive to L+M contrast modulations.
source: We find that within the LM cone contrast plane, V1 is most sensitive to L-M contrast modulations and least sensitive to L+M contrast modulations.
evidence: Supported by elliptical isoresponse contours with major axis aligned to L+M direction (Figure 6) and contrast response functions (Figure 2).

claim: Within V1, there is little to no change in chromatic sensitivity as a function of eccentricity.
source: Within V1, we observe little to no change in chromatic sensitivity as a function of eccentricity.
evidence: Supported by vertex-wise analysis showing minimal variation in QCM parameters with eccentricity (Figures 8, 9, Tables 1 and 2).

claim: Psychophysical evidence supports the existence of two cone-opponent mechanisms (S-(L+M) and L-M) and a luminance mechanism (L+M).
source: Psychophysical evidence supports the existence of two cone-opponent mechanisms, which represent differences between cone signals (S-(L+M) and L-M), and a luminance mechanism, which represents an additive combination (L+M) (Krauskopf et al., 1982; Stockman and Brainard, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to psychophysical literature (Krauskopf et al., 1982; Stockman and Brainard, 2010).

claim: Physiological evidence shows that cone signal recombination begins in the retina with correlates observed in retinal ganglion cells and lateral geniculate nucleus neurons.
source: Physiological evidence shows that this recombination begins in the retina with correlates observed in the responses of retinal ganglion cells and subsequently in the neurons of the lateral geniculate nucleus (De Valois et al., 1966; Derrington et al., 1984; Lennie and Movshon, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to physiological studies (De Valois et al., 1966; Derrington et al., 1984; Lennie and Movshon, 2005).

claim: Studies have not yet converged on a widely accepted quantitative parametric model of chromatic response properties of neurons in primate primary visual cortex (V1).
source: Studies focused on developing quantitative parametric models of the chromatic response properties of neurons in primary visual cortex of primates (area V1) have not yet converged on a widely accepted model (Johnson et al., 2004; Solomon and Lennie, 2005; Tailby et al., 2008; Horwitz and Hass, 2012; Weller and Horwitz, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies showing lack of consensus (Johnson et al., 2004; Solomon and Lennie, 2005; Tailby et al., 2008; Horwitz and Hass, 2012; Weller and Horwitz, 2018).

claim: Considerable heterogeneity of chromatic response properties exists across individual cortical neurons in V1.
source: In part, this is due to the considerable heterogeneity of chromatic response properties found across individual cortical neurons (Gegenfurtner, 2001; Lennie and Movshon, 2005; Solomon and Lennie, 2007; Shapley and Hawken, 2011; Horwitz, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies documenting heterogeneity (Gegenfurtner, 2001; Lennie and Movshon, 2005; Solomon and Lennie, 2007; Shapley and Hawken, 2011; Horwitz, 2020).

claim: The QCM has six free parameters: two that define the shape of the normalized elliptical isoresponse contour and four that define the Naka-Rushton equivalent contrast response function.
source: The QCM has six free parameters: two that define the shape of the normalized elliptical isoresponse contour and four that define the Naka-Rushton equivalent contrast response function.
evidence: This is a direct description of the model structure as defined by the authors.

claim: The GLM has 41 free parameters for modeling the experimental data.
source: The concatenated stimulus design matrix for a measurement set had a total of 41 regressors (20 direction/contrast pairs from Session 1, 20 direction/contrast pairs from Session 2, and a shared baseline regressor) and 7200 timepoints.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the GLM implementation.

claim: For all subjects and measurement sets, the angle of the isoresponse contours was oriented at approximately 45°.
source: We found that for all subjects and measurement sets, the angle of the isoresponse contours was oriented at approximately 45°.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6 displaying ellipse angles for all subjects and measurement sets.

claim: An ellipse angle of 45° indicates that V1 was least sensitive to stimuli modulated in the L+M direction and most sensitive to stimuli modulated in the L-M direction.
source: An ellipse angle of 45° indicates that V1 was least sensitive to stimuli modulated in the L+M direction, and most sensitive to stimuli modulated in the L-M direction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ellipse angle parameter based on the model definition.

claim: Across all subjects and measurement sets, the minor axis ratio parameters ranged between 0.15 and 0.25.
source: Across all subjects and measurement sets, the minor axis ratio parameters ranged between 0.15 and 0.25.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6 displaying minor axis ratios for all subjects and measurement sets.

claim: V1 was roughly five times more sensitive to modulations in the L-M direction than the L+M direction for the spatial and temporal properties of the stimuli used.
source: Thus, for the spatial and temporal properties of our modulations, V1 was roughly five times more sensitive to modulations in the L-M direction than the L+M direction.
evidence: This is calculated from the minor axis ratio values (approximately 0.2 = 1/5) shown in Figure 6.

claim: The stimuli used were spatially uniform (0 cycles per degree) chromatic temporal modulations presented using a block design.
source: To evaluate the QCM, three subjects underwent fMRI scanning while viewing stimuli consisting of spatially uniform (0 cycles per degree) chromatic temporal modulations, presented using a block design.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: Each 12 s block consisted of a 12 Hz bipolar temporal modulation in one of 8 chromatic directions and at one of 5 log-spaced contrast levels.
source: Each 12 s block consisted of a 12 Hz bipolar temporal modulation in one of 8 chromatic directions and at one of 5 log-spaced contrast levels.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design.

claim: Two complete measurement sets were collected for each subject to test for replicability of findings.
source: We collected two complete measurement sets (referred to as Measurement Set 1 and 2) for each subject, and fit the model to each set separately to test for the replicability of our findings.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design.

claim: For each chromatic direction, the V1 BOLD response generally increased with contrast.
source: For each chromatic direction, the V1 BOLD response generally increased with contrast, as expected.
evidence: Supported by contrast response functions shown in Figure 2 and supplementary figures.

claim: The rate at which V1 BOLD responses increase with contrast varied with chromatic direction.
source: The rate at which V1 BOLD responses increase with contrast varied with chromatic direction.
evidence: Supported by contrast response functions in Figure 2 showing different slopes for different chromatic directions.

claim: A modulation in the 45° direction required ~60% stimulus contrast to elicit a response of 0.6 while stimuli modulated in the −45° direction required only ~12% stimulus contrast to produce a similar response.
source: For example, a modulation in the 45° direction required ~60% stimulus contrast to elicit a response of 0.6 while stimuli modulated in the −45° direction required only ~12% stimulus contrast to produce a similar response.
evidence: This is observed from the contrast response functions in Figure 2.

claim: The median R2 value across runs was 0.41 for Measurement Set 1 and 0.32 for Measurement Set 2 for the GLM fits.
source: The median R2 value across runs was 0.41 for Measurement Set 1 and 0.32 for Measurement Set 2.
evidence: This is a direct report of the GLM fit quality for Subject 2.

claim: The QCM fit of the time course was of similar quality to the GLM fit.
source: The QCM fit of the time course was of similar quality to the GLM fit.
evidence: Supported by comparison of QCM and GLM fits shown in Figure 3 and cross-validation results in Figure 4.

claim: The QCM cross-validated R2 is essentially indistinguishable from the GLM cross-validated R2, although in all cases slightly higher.
source: Importantly, we see that the QCM cross-validated R2 is essentially indistinguishable from the GLM cross-validated R2, although in all cases slightly higher.
evidence: Supported by cross-validation results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The QCM is capable of generalizing well to unmeasured chromatic directions, with the requirement that the stimuli include chromatic directions and contrasts that adequately constrain the model parameters.
source: Therefore, the QCM is capable of generalizing well to unmeasured chromatic directions, with the requirement that the stimuli include chromatic directions and contrasts that adequately constrain the model parameters.
evidence: Supported by leave-session-out cross-validation results shown in Figure 5 and supplementary figures.

claim: Generalizations from Session 1 to Session 2 perform better than those from Session 2 to Session 1.
source: Overall, generalizations from Session 1 to Session 2 perform better than those from Session 2 to Session 1.
evidence: Observed from leave-session-out cross-validation results in Figure 5 and supplementary figures.

claim: Only Session 1 includes a chromatic direction close to the major axis of the ellipse, which better constrains the QCM fit.
source: This finding may reflect the particular set of chromatic directions presented in each session: only Session 1 includes a chromatic direction close to the major axis of the ellipse, which better constrains the QCM fit.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design and cross-validation results.

claim: The single nonlinearity of the QCM accurately captured the dependence of the GLM beta weight on equivalent contrast, with no apparent bias across chromatic directions.
source: For all subjects, the single nonlinearity accurately captured the dependence of the GLM beta weight on equivalent contrast, with no apparent bias across chromatic directions.
evidence: Supported by Figure 7 showing GLM beta weights plotted against equivalent contrast with QCM nonlinearity overlay.

claim: The stimuli did not drive the V1 response into the saturated regime.
source: Note that our stimuli did not drive the response into the saturated regime.
evidence: Observed from the Naka-Rushton functions in Figure 7 showing responses below saturation.

claim: Neither the ellipse angle nor the minor axis ratio parameters varied systematically within V1 as a function of eccentricity.
source: Apparent in the maps is that neither parameter varied systematically within V1, a feature of the data that is consistent across measurement sets and subjects.
evidence: Supported by cortical surface maps in Figure 8 and scatter plots in Figure 9.

claim: Outside of V1, the R2 values were markedly lower and there was higher variability in the QCM parameters.
source: Outside of V1, the R2 values were markedly lower, and there was higher variability in the QCM parameters.
evidence: Observed from cortical surface maps in Figure 8.

claim: The overall change in parameter values from 0° to 20° eccentricity was small compared to the vertical spread of values at each eccentricity.
source: The overall change in parameter values from 0° to 20°, however, was small compared to the vertical spread of values at each eccentricity.
evidence: Observed from scatter plots in Figure 9 showing parameter values versus eccentricity.

claim: Engel et al., 1997 found that the V1 BOLD fMRI signal was maximally sensitive to L-M stimulus modulations.
source: Notably, Engel et al., 1997 conducted a pioneering study that varied the chromatic content and temporal frequency of stimuli and observed that the V1 BOLD fMRI signal was maximally sensitive to L-M stimulus modulations.
evidence: This is a citation to prior work by Engel et al., 1997.

claim: Elliptical isoresponse contours have been successfully used to model chromatic isoresponse contours in prior psychophysical, electrophysiological, and fMRI experiments.
source: The use of elliptical isoresponse contours is motivated by prior psychophysical (Poirson et al., 1990; Knoblauch and Maloney, 1996), electrophysiological (Horwitz and Hass, 2012), and fMRI experiments (Engel et al., 1997) which have successfully used ellipses to model chromatic isoresponse contours.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies (Poirson et al., 1990; Knoblauch and Maloney, 1996; Horwitz and Hass, 2012; Engel et al., 1997).

claim: The QCM assumes that the aspect ratio and orientation of elliptical isoresponse contours do not change as a function of the response level; only the overall scale of the ellipse changes.
source: Importantly, the QCM assumes that the aspect ratio and orientation of elliptical isoresponse contours do not change as a function of the response level; only the overall scale of the ellipse changes.
evidence: This is a fundamental assumption of the QCM model as defined by the authors.

claim: The minor axis of the elliptical isoresponse contour corresponds to the chromatic direction that requires the least amount of cone contrast to produce an equal neuronal response, and is therefore the most sensitive chromatic direction.
source: The minor axis of the elliptical isoresponse contour corresponds to the chromatic direction that requires the least amount of cone contrast to produce this equal neuronal response, and is therefore the most sensitive chromatic direction.
evidence: This is a definition of the minor axis parameter in the QCM model.

claim: The major axis of the elliptical isoresponse contour corresponds to the direction of least sensitivity.
source: The major axis corresponds to the direction of least sensitivity.
evidence: This is a definition of the major axis parameter in the QCM model.

claim: Three subjects (age 23, 25, and 26 years; two female) participated in the fMRI experiment.
source: Three subjects (age 23, 25, and 26 years; two female) took part in the fMRI experiment.
evidence: This is a direct description of the study participants.

claim: All subjects had normal or corrected to normal acuity and normal color vision.
source: All subjects had normal or corrected to normal acuity and normal color vision.
evidence: This is a direct description of subject inclusion criteria.

claim: All subjects passed the Ishihara pseudoischromatic plates test with no errors.
source: Subjects were tested for color vision deficiencies in a separate session, using the Ishihara pseudoischromatic plates (Ishihara, 1977). All subjects passed with no errors.
evidence: This is a direct report of color vision testing results.

claim: The research was approved by the University of Pennsylvania Institutional Review Board.
source: The research was approved by the University of Pennsylvania Institutional Review Board.
evidence: This is a statement of ethical approval.

claim: All subjects gave informed written consent and were financially compensated for their participation.
source: All subjects gave informed written consent and were financially compensated for their participation.
evidence: This is a statement of ethical procedures.

claim: The experimental procedures for Measurement Set 1 were preregistered at https://osf.io/wgfzy/.
source: The experimental procedures for Measurement Set 1 were preregistered (https://osf.io/wgfzy/), and an addendum describes the replication Measurement Set 2 (https://osf.io/zw6jp/).
evidence: This is a statement of preregistration.

claim: All stimuli were generated using a digital light synthesis device (OneLight Spectra).
source: All stimuli were generated using a digital light synthesis device (OneLight Spectra).
evidence: This is a direct description of the stimulus generation equipment.

claim: The OneLight Spectra device allows for the mixture of 56 independent primaries with a FWHM of ~16 nm and a refresh rate of 100 Hz.
source: This device produces desired spectra through the use of a digital micro-mirror device chip that in the configuration we used allows for the mixture of 56 independent primaries with a FWHM of ~16 nm and a refresh rate of 100 Hz.
evidence: This is a direct description of the device specifications.

claim: Stimuli were generated to evoke specific photoreceptor responses through the use of silent substitution.
source: Stimuli were generated to evoke specific photoreceptor responses through the use of silent substitution (Estévez and Spekreijse, 1982).
evidence: This is a direct description of the stimulus generation method with citation.

claim: Silent substitution operates on the principle that there exist sets of light spectra that, when exchanged, selectively modulate the activity of specified cone photoreceptors.
source: Silent substitution operates on the principle that there exist sets of light spectra that, when exchanged, selectively modulate the activity of specified cone photoreceptors.
evidence: This is a definition of the silent substitution technique.

claim: The stimuli account for differences in the cone fundamentals between the fovea and the periphery by treating the L, M, and S cones in the 2- and 15-degree CIE physiologically-based cone fundamentals as six classes of photoreceptors.
source: The stimuli account for differences in the cone fundamentals between the fovea and the periphery. This was done by treating the L, M, and S cones in the 2- and 15-degree CIE physiologically-based cone fundamentals (CIE, 2007) as six classes of photoreceptors.
evidence: This is a direct description of the stimulus design procedure.

claim: The procedure of accounting for eccentricity-dependent cone fundamentals has the effect of creating light spectra that reduce differences in the L-, M-, and S-cone contrasts produced across the retina.
source: Our procedure has the effect of creating light spectra that reduce differences in the L-, M-, and S-cone contrasts produced across the retina.
evidence: This is an explanation of the effect of the stimulus design procedure.

claim: The cone fundamentals were tailored to the age of each subject to account for age-related differences in typical lens density.
source: The cone fundamentals were tailored to the age of each subject, to account for age-related differences in typical lens density (CIE, 2007).
evidence: This is a direct description of the stimulus calibration procedure.

claim: Spectroradiometric measurements of the stimuli were made before and after each experimental session.
source: Spectroradiometric measurements of the stimuli were made before and after each experimental session.
evidence: This is a direct description of the measurement validation procedure.

claim: A correction procedure was run in which the spectral power distribution of the modulation in each chromatic direction were adjusted to minimize the difference between the measured and desired cone contrasts for the 2- and 15-degree cone fundamentals.
source: During the measurements made prior to the experiment, a correction procedure was run in which the spectral power distribution of the modulation in each chromatic direction were adjusted to minimize the difference between the measured and desired cone contrasts for the 2- and 15-degree cone fundamentals.
evidence: This is a direct description of the calibration procedure.

claim: The background had a nominal chromaticity of x = 0.459, y = 0.478, and luminance Y = 426 cd/m^2.
source: We refer to the reference spectrum used to calculate this relative change in cone excitations as the background (nominal chromaticity; x = 0.459, y = 0.478, luminance Y = 426 cd/m^2; chromaticity and luminance computed with respect to the XYZ 10° physiologically-relevant color matching functions, as provided at https://cvrl.org).
evidence: This is a direct specification of the background stimulus properties.

claim: All stimuli were modulated at 12 Hz temporal frequency.
source: All stimuli were modulated at 12 Hz (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is a direct specification of the temporal frequency used.

claim: The stimuli were spatially uniform full-field temporal modulations with a radius of 30° visual angle.
source: All stimuli were spatially uniform (0 c.p.d.), full-field temporal modulations with a radius of 30° visual angle.
evidence: This is a direct specification of the spatial properties of the stimuli.

claim: Eight chromatic directions were tested: −45°, −22.5°, 0°, 22.5°, 45°, 67.5°, 90°, and 112.5°.
source: In total, we tested the eight chromatic directions: −45°, −22.5°, 0°, 22.5°,45°, 67.5°, 90°, and 112.5°.
evidence: This is a direct specification of the chromatic directions tested.

claim: The −45°, 0°, 45°, and 90° directions correspond to L-M, L-cone isolating, L+M, and M-cone isolating directions, respectively.
source: The −45°, 0°, 45°, and 90° directions correspond to L-M, L-cone isolating, L+M, and M-cone isolating directions, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct specification of the chromatic direction labels.

claim: For all chromatic directions, the spectra were designed to produce constant S-cone contrast.
source: For all chromatic directions, the spectra were designed to produce constant S-cone contrast.
evidence: This is a direct specification of the stimulus design constraint.

claim: Five contrast levels were tested for all directions, selected to be log spaced relative to the maximum contrast used, at relative contrasts of 100, 50, 25, 12.5, and 6.25 percent.
source: For all directions, we tested five contrast levels. The contrast levels tested for each chromatic direction were selected to be log spaced relative to the maximum contrast used. The relative contrasts were 100, 50, 25, 12.5, and 6.25 percent.
evidence: This is a direct specification of the contrast levels tested.

claim: A 0 contrast reference condition in which the background without modulation was presented was also measured.
source: We also measured a 0 contrast reference condition in which the background without modulation was presented.
evidence: This is a direct description of the baseline condition.

claim: Within a block, modulations were ramped on and off using a 500 ms half-cosine.
source: Within a block, modulations were ramped on and off using a 500 ms half-cosine.
evidence: This is a direct description of the temporal envelope of the stimuli.

claim: During each functional run, subjects engaged in an attention task that consisted of pressing a button every time the stimulus dimmed.
source: During each functional run, subjects engaged in an attention task. This task consisted of pressing a button every time the stimulus dimmed (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is a direct description of the attention task.

claim: Each attentional event lasted for 500 ms.
source: Each attentional event lasted for 500 ms.
evidence: This is a direct specification of the attention event duration.

claim: The probability of an attentional event occurring in a block was 66% in Measurement Set 1 and 33% in Measurement Set 2.
source: The probability of an attentional event occurring in a block was 66% in Measurement Set 1 and a 33% in Measurement Set 2.
evidence: This is a direct specification of the attention event probability.

claim: All subjects responded to 100% of the attentional events throughout all runs and sessions.
source: All subjects responded to 100% of the attentional events throughout all runs and sessions.
evidence: This is a direct report of subject performance on the attention task.

claim: Across both sessions and measurement sets, a total of 960 blocks per subject were collected.
source: Across both sessions and measurements sets, we collected a total of 960 blocks per subject.
evidence: This is a direct specification of the total number of blocks collected.

claim: MRI scans made use of the Human Connectome Project LifeSpan protocol (VD13D) implemented on a 3-Tesla Siemens Prisma with a 64-channel Siemens head coil.
source: MRI scans made use of the Human Connectome Project LifeSpan protocol (VD13D) implemented on a 3-Tesla Siemens Prisma with a 64-channel Siemens head coil.
evidence: This is a direct description of the MRI acquisition protocol.

claim: A T1-weighted MPRAGE anatomical image was acquired for each subject in axial orientation with 0.8 mm isotropic voxels, TR = 2.4 s, TE = 2.22 ms, TI = 1000 ms, FoV = 256 mm, flip angle = 8°.
source: A T1-weighted, 3D, magnetization-prepared rapid gradient-echo (MPRAGE) anatomical image was acquired for each subject in axial orientation with 0.8 mm isotropic voxels, repetition time (TR) = 2.4 s, echo time (TE) = 2.22 ms, inversion time (TI) = 1000 ms, field of view (FoV) = 256 mm, flip angle = 8°.
evidence: This is a direct specification of the anatomical imaging parameters.

claim: BOLD fMRI data were obtained over 72 axial slices with 2 mm isotropic voxels with multi-band = 8, TR = 800 ms, TE = 37 ms, FOV = 208 mm, flip angle = 52°.
source: BOLD fMRI data were obtained over 72 axial slices with 2 mm isotropic voxels with multi-band = 8, TR = 800 ms, TE = 37 ms, FOV = 208 mm, flip angle = 52°.
evidence: This is a direct specification of the functional imaging parameters.

claim: Visual stimuli were presented through an MRI compatible eyepiece to the right eye of the subject.
source: During MRI scanning, subjects were supine inside the magnet. Visual stimuli were presented through an MRI compatible eyepiece to the right eye of the subject.
evidence: This is a direct description of the stimulus presentation method.

claim: Stimuli were delivered from the digital light synthesizer through a randomized optical fiber cable.
source: Stimuli were delivered from the digital light synthesizer through a randomized optical fiber cable (Fiberoptics Technology Inc).
evidence: This is a direct description of the stimulus delivery method.

claim: The randomization of the fiber optic cable helped to minimize any spatial inhomogeneities in the spectrum of the stimulus.
source: The randomization of the fiber optic cable helped to minimize any spatial inhomogeneities in the spectrum of the stimulus.
evidence: This is an explanation of the purpose of using a randomized fiber optic cable.

claim: Both anatomical and functional data were preprocessed according to the HCP minimal preprocessing pipeline.
source: Both anatomical and functional data were preprocessed according to the HCP minimal preprocessing pipeline (Glasser et al., 2013)
evidence: This is a direct description of the preprocessing pipeline with citation.

claim: The functional data were passed through the ICAFIX pipeline, which uses independent component analysis and noise/not-noise classification to denoise the time course.
source: Finally, the functional data were passed through the ICAFIX pipeline, which uses independent component analysis and noise/not-noise classification to denoise the time course.
evidence: This is a direct description of the denoising procedure.

claim: Time-point censoring was performed based on motion estimates using a modified version of Power et al., 2014.
source: Next, we time-point censored the time series of all voxels based on the motion estimates. This was done using a modified version of Power et al., 2014.
evidence: This is a direct description of the motion censoring procedure with citation.

claim: Time points with frame-wise displacement (FD) > 0.5 were censored along with three contiguous TRs centered on that time point.
source: We censored three contiguous TRs centered on any time point with an FD > 0.5.
evidence: This is a direct specification of the motion censoring threshold.

claim: Polynomial detrending was applied by fitting a fifth order polynomial to the time course from each voxel and subtracting it from the signal.
source: Finally, we applied polynomial detrending by fitting a fifth order polynomial to the time course from each voxel and subtracting it from the signal.
evidence: This is a direct description of the detrending procedure.

claim: Retinotopic regions of interest were defined using the anatomical template neuropythy.
source: Retinotopic regions of interest (ROI) were defined using the anatomical template neuropythy (Benson et al., 2014) which provides eccentricity and polar angle maps for V1, V2, and V3.
evidence: This is a direct description of the ROI definition method with citation.

claim: A V1 ROI was defined using voxels in area V1 between 0–20° eccentricity and 0–180° polar angle.
source: From this atlas, we defined a V1 ROI using the voxels in area V1 between 0–20° eccentricity and 0–180° polar angle.
evidence: This is a direct specification of the V1 ROI definition.

claim: The eccentricity upper bound of the ROI was set to 20° to provide a conservative boundary to ensure that only stimulated vertices were analyzed.
source: We set the eccentricity upper bound of the ROI to be 20° to provide a conservative boundary to ensure that we only analyzed stimulated vertices.
evidence: This is an explanation of the rationale for the ROI boundary.

claim: Subject-specific hemodynamic response functions were derived for each subject and measurement set using all functional runs within a measurement set.
source: We derived subject-specific hemodynamic response functions (HRFs) for each subject and measurement set. The HRF was derived using all the functional runs within a measurement set, using the V1 region of interest median data.
evidence: This is a direct description of the HRF estimation procedure.

claim: The HRF model was composed of the first three components of the 'FLOBS' basis set.
source: The HRF model was composed of the first three components of the 'FLOBS' basis set (Woolrich et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a direct specification of the HRF model with citation.

claim: An ordinary least squares regression with a stimulus design matrix was used to fit the GLM.
source: We used an ordinary least squares regression with a stimulus design matrix that described the stimulus order of a run.
evidence: This is a direct description of the GLM fitting procedure.

claim: The concatenated stimulus design matrix for a measurement set had 7200 timepoints.
source: The concatenated stimulus design matrix for a measurement set had a total of 41 regressors (20 direction/contrast pairs from Session 1, 20 direction/contrast pairs from Session 2, and a shared baseline regressor) and 7200 timepoints.
evidence: This is a direct specification of the design matrix dimensions.

claim: Error bars and error regions in all figures are 68 percent confidence intervals obtained using bootstrap analysis with 200 iterations.
source: The error bars and error regions in all figures are the 68 percent confidence intervals. We used 68% confidence intervals as this approximates +/- 1 SEM for a normal distribution. The percentiles we use to estimate error are the result of a bootstrap analysis... We performed 200 bootstrap iterations and identified the 68% percent confidence interval from the bootstrap results.
evidence: This is a direct description of the error estimation procedure.

claim: A leave-runs-out cross-validation strategy was employed to evaluate model performance.
source: To evaluate model performance, we employed a leave-runs-out cross-validation strategy.
evidence: This is a direct description of the cross-validation procedure.

claim: For leave-runs-out cross-validation, runs from Session 1 and Session 2 were randomly paired and held out, with models fit to the remaining 18 runs.
source: For each cross-validation iteration, runs from Session 1 and Session 2 were randomly paired within the same measurement set. These pairs of runs were held out and the models were fit to the remaining 18 runs.
evidence: This is a direct description of the cross-validation procedure.

claim: The average R^2 value across 10 cross-validation iterations was used to compare models.
source: The average R^2 value across the 10 cross-validation iterations was used to compare models.
evidence: This is a direct description of the model comparison metric.

claim: A leave-session-out cross-validation was implemented to evaluate the generalizability of the QCM.
source: To evaluate the generalizability of the QCM, we implemented a leave-session-out cross-validation.
evidence: This is a direct description of the generalization testing procedure.

claim: For leave-session-out cross-validation, the QCM was fit to Sessions 1 and 2 separately and evaluated on how well the parameters predicted responses to stimulus directions in the held-out session.
source: Within each measurement set, we fit the QCM to Sessions 1 and 2 separately and evaluated how well the parameters of the model predicted responses to stimulus directions in the held-out session.
evidence: This is a direct description of the leave-session-out cross-validation procedure.

claim: Cortical surface maps were generated by fitting the QCM within a single vertex to the concatenated time course from all runs in a measurement set, repeated for all vertices within the visual areas template map.
source: To generate the surface parameter maps, we fit the QCM, within a single vertex, to the concatenated time course from all runs in a measurement set. We repeat this fit for all vertices within the visual areas template map from neuropythy (Benson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a direct description of the surface map generation procedure.

claim: The QCM was fit to data using the MATLAB function fmincon to minimize the root mean squared error between the actual fMRI time course and the QCM prediction.
source: We fit QCM the model to the concatenated time series for both sessions within a measurement set for each subject. The data were fit using the MATLAB function fmincon to find a set of model parameters that minimize the difference between the actual fMRI time course and the QCM prediction of the time course, computed as the root mean squared error.
evidence: This is a direct description of the model fitting procedure.

claim: All code used to perform analyses is publicly available in a GitHub repository.
source: All code used to perform analyses in this paper may be found in our public GitHub repository: https://github.com/BrainardLab/LFContrastAnalysis_eLife.git (copy archived at swh:1:rev:c9b4cbe72e69e4d3d623ec8b7fc62076e2fe1a22, Barnett, 2021).
evidence: This is a statement of code availability.

claim: Engel et al., 1997 found that for low temporal frequencies the psychophysical isothreshold and BOLD fMRI isoresponse contours in the LM contrast plane were well-described as ellipses and had similar shapes.
source: For example, an approach to studying chromatic sensitivity is to characterize the isothreshold contour, which specifies the set of stimulus modulations that are equally detectable. Engel et al., 1997 took this approach and found that for low temporal frequencies the psychophysical isothreshold and BOLD fMRI isoresponse contours in the LM contrast plane were well-described as ellipses and had similar shapes.
evidence: This is a citation to findings from Engel et al., 1997.

claim: Psychophysical isothreshold contours remain well-described by ellipses at higher temporal frequencies, but their orientation changes to favor L+M sensitivity over L-M sensitivity.
source: As they note, although psychophysical isothreshold contours remain well-described by ellipses at higher temporal frequencies, their orientation changes to favor L+M sensitivity over L-M sensitivity.
evidence: This is a citation to findings from Engel et al., 1997 and related literature.

claim: A quadratic isoresponse contour can be produced by a quadratic mechanism that computes a sum of the squared responses of two underlying linear mechanisms.
source: More generally, a quadratic isorepsonse contour can be produced by a quadratic mechanism that computes a sum of the squared responses of two underlying linear mechanisms, where the output of each linear mechanism is a weighted sum of L- and M-cone contrasts (Poirson et al., 1990).
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation with citation to Poirson et al., 1990.

claim: The isoresponse contours do not uniquely determine the sensitivity of the underlying linear mechanisms, even within the QCM together with the assumption that there are two such mechanisms.
source: Note, however, that other pairs of underlying mechanisms are also consistent with the same elliptical isoresponse contours (Poirson et al., 1990), so that our isoresponse contours do not uniquely determine the sensitivity of the underlying linear mechanisms, even within the QCM together with the assumption that there are two such mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on theoretical considerations with citation to Poirson et al., 1990.

claim: The Linear Channels Model (LCM) accounts for the data about as well as the QCM.
source: To illustrate this point, we developed and fit an alternate model, the Linear Channels Model (LCM), a variation on the Brouwer and Heeger channel model (Brouwer and Heeger, 2009; Kim et al., 2020), that accounts for our data about as well as the QCM (see Appendix 1; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by cross-validation results in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The best fitting isoresponse contours found with the LCM approximate the ellipse found using the QCM, but are not perfectly elliptical.
source: The best fitting isoresponse contours found with the LCM, which could in principle deviate considerably from an ellipse, none-the-less approximate the ellipse we found using the QCM, but are not perfectly elliptical (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison of isoresponse contours in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A form of the QCM with the angle constrained to 0 degrees resulted in a noticeably lower cross-validated R2 compared to all other models tested.
source: To address this, we fit and cross-validated a form of the QCM with the angle constrained to 0 degrees. This resulted in a noticeably lower cross-validated R2 for this model as compared to all other models we tested (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, labeled at 'QCM locked')
evidence: Supported by cross-validation results in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The spatially uniform (0 c.p.d.) chromatic modulations at 12 Hz could drive 'color', 'luminance' and 'color-luminance' cells as described by Johnson et al., 2001, depending on the particular chromatic direction.
source: Our stimuli were large, spatially uniform (effectively 0 c.p.d.) chromatic modulations that were temporally modulated at 12 Hz. These stimuli could drive 'color', 'luminance' and 'color-luminance' cells as described by Johnson et al., 2001, depending on the particular chromatic direction.
evidence: This is an inference based on stimulus properties and citation to Johnson et al., 2001.

claim: The 0 c.p.d. stimuli would presumably produce strong responses in 'color' cells for the L-M direction, given that these cells are thought to behave as low-pass filters in the spatial domain and have unoriented receptive fields.
source: The 0 c.p.d. stimuli would presumably produce strong responses in the 'color' cells for our L-M direction, given that these cells are thought to behave as low-pass filters in the spatial domain and have unoriented receptive fields.
evidence: This is an inference based on known properties of color cells.

claim: At 0.1 c.p.d., firing rates for color cells are roughly 5x times higher than the firing rates for luminance and color-luminance cells according to Schluppeck and Engel, 2002.
source: Schluppeck and Engel, 2002 plot the spatial frequency response function estimated from the data from Johnson et al., 2001. These functions plot the average firing rate as a function of spatial frequency for the color, color-luminance, and luminance cells. Taking the lowest spatial frequency present in the dataset (0.1 c.p.d.), firing rates for color cells are roughly 5x times higher than the firing rates for luminance and color-luminance cells.
evidence: This is a citation to findings from Schluppeck and Engel, 2002 analyzing data from Johnson et al., 2001.

claim: The average minor axis ratio of approximately 0.2 indicates V1 is roughly five times more sensitive to L-M than to L+M, which is the same as the ratio of firing rates for color cells versus luminance and color-luminance cells at low spatial frequencies.
source: This is the same as our average minor axis ratio which indicates V1 is roughly five times more sensitive to L-M than to L+M.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the QCM results to electrophysiological data.

claim: The data do not distinguish the extent to which the response properties of the BOLD signals measured in V1 are inherited from the LGN or are shaped by processing within V1.
source: It is also important to note that our data do not distinguish the extent to which the response properties of the BOLD signals we measure in V1 are inherited from the LGN or are shaped by processing within V1.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in interpreting the results.

claim: The spatiotemporal properties of the stimuli would robustly drive cells in the LGN that project to V1.
source: The spatiotemporal properties of our stimuli would robustly drive cells in cell in the LGN that project to V1 (Lankheet et al., 1998).
evidence: This is an inference based on stimulus properties with citation to Lankheet et al., 1998.

claim: The V1 sensitivities found from fitting the QCM may be inherited from areas prior to V1 or could be affected by feedback from other cortical areas.
source: As such, the V1 sensitivities found from fitting the QCM may be inherited from areas prior to V1. In principle, they could also be affected by feedback from other cortical areas.
evidence: This is speculation about possible sources of the measured responses.

claim: Quadratic models have been used to characterize the isoresponse properties of individual neurons in macaque V1, with roughly half of neurons best fit by quadratic isoresponse surfaces and the other half by linear models.
source: Finally, it is interesting to observe that quadratic models have been used to characterize the isoresponse properties of individual neurons in macaque V1 (Horwitz and Hass, 2012). Roughly half of the neurons tested in this paper were best fit by quadratic isoresponse surfaces (in the L-, M-, and S-cone contrast space) while the other half were well fit by a linear model whose isoresponse surfaces were parallel planes.
evidence: This is a citation to findings from Horwitz and Hass, 2012.

claim: Of the quadratic isoresponse surfaces in individual neurons, some were ellipsoidal while others were hyperbolic.
source: Of the quadratic isoresponse surfaces, some were ellipsoidal while others were hyperbolic.
evidence: This is a citation to findings from Horwitz and Hass, 2012.

claim: Mullen et al., 2007 and Vanni et al., 2006 report a decrease in the V1 response to L-M modulations with eccentricity, while the response to L+M remains roughly constant.
source: Both Mullen et al., 2007 and Vanni et al., 2006 report a decrease in the V1 response to L-M modulations with eccentricity, while the response to L+M remains roughly constant.
evidence: This is a citation to findings from Mullen et al., 2007 and Vanni et al., 2006.

claim: The findings of Mullen et al., 2007 and Vanni et al., 2006 differ from the current study's result of no change in chromatic sensitivity with eccentricity.
source: This differs from our result, and the size of the effects in these papers are large enough that we would expect that if they were present in our data they would be visible in the analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1
evidence: This is a comparison of the current results to prior findings.

claim: Mullen et al., 2007 and Vanni et al., 2006 speculate that the mechanism underlying decreased L-M sensitivity with eccentricity is non-selective (random) connections between L and M cones and retinal ganglion cell receptive fields.
source: Both speculate that the mechanism underlying this observation is non-selective (random) connections between L and M cones and retinal ganglion cell receptive fields.
evidence: This is a citation to speculation from Mullen et al., 2007 and Vanni et al., 2006.

claim: If connections between cones and ganglion cells are non-selective, L-M sensitivity would be expected to decrease with eccentricity because receptive field pooling area increases with distance from the fovea.
source: If these connections are non-selective, L-M sensitivity would be expected to decrease with eccentricity. This is because the area in which receptive fields pool cone inputs increases with distance from the fovea, progressively reducing the likelihood that random L- and M-cone inputs to the center and surround will produce chromatic opponency (Lennie et al., 1991; Mullen and Kingdom, 1996; Wool et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation with citations to Lennie et al., 1991; Mullen and Kingdom, 1996; Wool et al., 2018.

claim: D'Souza et al., 2016 find, for the majority of spatial frequencies studied, no change in L-M response relative to the response to isochromatic luminance modulations with eccentricity.
source: In contrast, D'Souza et al., 2016 find, for the majority of spatial frequencies studied, no change in L-M response relative to the response to isochromatic luminance modulations.
evidence: This is a citation to findings from D'Souza et al., 2016.

claim: D'Souza et al., 2016 take their result as supporting the idea that connections between cones and some classes of ganglion cells are selective for cone type and preserve chromatic sensitivity across the retina.
source: Following the same line of reasoning as Mullen et al., 2007 and Vanni et al., 2006 but reaching the opposite conclusion, D'Souza et al., 2016 take their result as supporting the idea that connections between cones and some classes of ganglion cells are selective for cone type and preserve chromatic sensitivity across the retina.
evidence: This is a citation to the interpretation from D'Souza et al., 2016.

claim: Variation in macular pigment and photopigment optical density can produce eccentricity-dependent deviations in the degree of actual cone contrast reaching the photoreceptors.
source: One such factor is the changes in cone spectral sensitivity with eccentricity, caused primarily by variation in macular pigment and photopigment optical density. Variation in macular pigment and photopigment optical density can produce eccentricity-dependent deviations in the degree of actual cone contrast reaching the photoreceptors.
evidence: This is an explanation of a potential confound based on known optical properties of the eye.

claim: Prior studies examining eccentricity effects do not account for variation in macular pigment and photopigment optical density.
source: Prior studies do not account for this variation, leading to the possibility that effects of eccentricity on sensitivity are due to receptoral, rather than post-receptoral mechanisms.
evidence: This is a critique of prior studies based on methodological considerations.

claim: In the current study, spectral modulations were designed to produce the same contrasts in both 2-degree and 15-degree cone fundamentals, which reduces the change in cone contrast with eccentricity.
source: In our study, we designed spectral modulations that produce the same contrasts in both 2-degree and 15-degree cone fundamentals (see Materials and methods and Tables 5–7). This reduces the change in cone contrast with eccentricity for our stimuli.
evidence: This is a description of a methodological feature of the current study.

claim: The lack of variation in chromatic sensitivity with eccentricity in the data is parsimoniously explained by retinal output that preserves chromatic sensitivity with eccentricity.
source: Although changes in sensitivity with eccentricity can be caused by mechanisms at many levels of the visual system, the lack of such variation in our data is parsimoniously explained by retinal output that preserves chromatic sensitivity with eccentricity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results.

claim: Studies show random or close to random inputs from L- and M-cones to midget ganglion cell centers in the retinal periphery.
source: This interpretation is challenged by studies that show random (Wool et al., 2018) or close to random (Field et al., 2010) inputs from L- and M-cones to midget ganglion cell centers in the retinal periphery.
evidence: This is a citation to findings from Wool et al., 2018 and Field et al., 2010.

claim: Not all studies of midget cell chromatic responses or their parvocellular LGN counterparts agree with non-selective wiring.
source: Not all studies of midget cell chromatic responses or their parvocelluar LGN counterparts agree with non-selective wiring (Reid and Shapley, 1992; Martin et al., 2001; Martin et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a citation to findings from Reid and Shapley, 1992; Martin et al., 2001; Martin et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012.

claim: One possible cortical mechanism that could compensate for reduced L-M signal-to-noise ratio with eccentricity is supra-threshold compensation for reduced signals.
source: One possible cortical mechanism that could compensate for the reduced L-M signal-to-noise ratio with eccentricity as predicted by random wiring models is supra-threshold compensation for reduced signals.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: Mechanisms of supra-threshold compensation have been postulated in the domain of contrast perception and anomalous trichromatic vision.
source: Mechanisms of this sort have been postulated in the domain of contrast perception (Georgeson and Sullivan, 1975) and anomalous trichromatic vision (Boehm et al., 2014; Tregillus et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a citation to prior work on compensation mechanisms (Georgeson and Sullivan, 1975; Boehm et al., 2014; Tregillus et al., 2021).

claim: A differential change in stimulus integration area across chromatic directions and with eccentricity is not supported by fMRI population receptive field measurements for modulations in different chromatic directions in V1.
source: Another possibility is a differential change in stimulus integration area across chromatic directions and with eccentricity. However, this latter possibility is not supported by fMRI population receptive field (pRF) measurements for modulations in different chromatic directions in V1 (Welbourne et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a citation to findings from Welbourne et al., 2018 that rule out a particular explanation.

claim: The QCM may be generalized to handle stimuli in the full L-, M-, and S-cone contrast space by replacing the elliptical isoresponse contours with ellipsoidal isoresponse surfaces.
source: In our study, we only measured responses to stimuli confined to the LM contrast plane. A more general account of chromatic contrast sensitivity requires modulating stimuli in all three-dimension of the full L-, M-, and S-cone contrast space. The QCM may be generalized in a straightforward manner to handle this expanded stimulus set by replacing the elliptical isoresponse contours with ellipsoidal isoresponse surfaces, but we have yet to test this generalization.
evidence: This is a proposal for future work based on the current model structure.

claim: The QCM could be readily fit to data from modulations at various temporal frequencies to observe how chromatic sensitivity changes with temporal frequency.
source: Another way in which the QCM may be generalized, even within the LM contrast plane, is to consider modulations at other temporal frequencies. In our experiment, we fixed the temporal modulation of the stimulus at 12 Hz. The QCM could be readily fit to data from modulations at various other temporal frequencies with the goal of observing how the chromatic sensitivity changes.
evidence: This is a proposal for future work.

claim: If the response to temporal frequency mixtures can be predicted via a simple rule of combination, establishing the QCM parameters for a well-chosen set of temporal frequencies would enable prediction of the BOLD response to chromatic stimuli modulated with complex temporal sequences.
source: With this, one could further examine the BOLD response to mixtures of different temporal frequency modulations. This is particularly interesting in that any arbitrary complex temporal modulation can be decomposed into an additive mixture of modulations at different temporal frequencies and phases (Bracewell, 1978). If the response to temporal frequency mixtures can be predicted via a simple rule of combination (such as linearity), establishing the QCM parameters for a well-chosen set of temporal frequencies would enable prediction of the BOLD response to chromatic stimuli modulated with complex temporal sequences.
evidence: This is speculation about potential generalization of the model with citation to Bracewell, 1978.

claim: Examining how the QCM fits change with changing spatial frequencies might allow for models of the BOLD response to arbitrary complex spatial stimuli.
source: Just as we had a fixed temporal frequency in our experiment, the stimulus presented also had a fixed spatial frequency (0 c.p.d.). Similar to the temporal domain, complex spatial images can be broken down into a combination of oriented two-dimensional sine wave patterns at single spatial frequencies and phases. Examining how the QCM fits change with changing spatial frequencies might allow for models of the BOLD response to arbitrary complex spatial stimuli.
evidence: This is speculation about potential generalization of the model.

claim: Recent work has developed quantitative forward models of the BOLD response of early visual cortex to a variety of achromatic modulations with different spatial patterns.
source: Consistent with this general goal, recent work has developed quantitative forward models of the BOLD response of early visual cortex to a variety of achromatic modulations with different spatial patterns (Kay et al., 2013a; Kay et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is a citation to prior work by Kay et al., 2013a; Kay et al., 2013b.

claim: How forward models of BOLD response should be generalized to handle chromatic modulations is not known.
source: These models have sequential stages of processing that operate on an input image and transform it into a model of the BOLD response. How such models should be generalized to handle chromatic modulations is not known.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in current knowledge.

claim: If the QCM holds for other spatial frequencies, such a result would place important constraints on the appropriate generalization for forward models to incorporate color.
source: If the QCM holds for other spatial frequencies, such a result would place important constraints on the appropriate generalization for such forward models to incorporate color.
evidence: This is speculation about the implications of potential future findings.
